framework_version: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark (v4.x control numbering)
source_note: Conditions and remediation follow the CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark. Clause numbers are given for traceability and should be re-confirmed against your licensed copy of the benchmark for the exact IOS train you audit; rules whose clause could not be pinned exactly carry a section-level control_ref and a note.

rules.title: Enable 'aaa new-model'
rules.description: AAA must be enabled so that authentication, authorization and accounting for device access are centrally defined rather than falling back to line-local passwords.
rules.rationale: Without 'aaa new-model' the device uses legacy line authentication, which cannot enforce per-user accountability, centralised credential revocation, or command accounting.

remediation.summary: Enable the AAA subsystem, then define authentication methods before disconnecting.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 1.1.1 Enable 'aaa new-model'
rules.notes: Enabling AAA changes login behaviour immediately. Configure 'aaa authentication login' with a local fallback in the same session to avoid lockout.

rules.title: Set 'transport input ssh' for 'line vty' connections
rules.description: VTY lines must accept SSH only. Telnet and the other legacy transports carry credentials and session data in cleartext.
rules.rationale: Telnet transmits usernames, passwords and configuration in cleartext. Anyone able to observe the management path can capture privileged credentials and replay them.

remediation.summary: Restrict every VTY line to the SSH transport.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 1.2.2 Set 'transport input ssh' for 'line vty' connections
rules.notes: Evaluated worst-case across all 'line vty' blocks: if any block permits a cleartext transport, the control fails.

rules.title: Set 'exec-timeout' to 10 minutes or less on 'line vty'
rules.description: Idle VTY sessions must be torn down automatically. An exec-timeout of 0 disables the timeout entirely and is explicitly non-compliant.
rules.rationale: An unattended, authenticated session left open on a workstation or terminal server is a ready-made privileged foothold. 'exec-timeout 0 0' means the session never expires.

remediation.summary: Set an idle timeout of 10 minutes or less on every VTY line.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 1.2.9 Set 'exec-timeout' less than or equal to 10 minutes 'line vty'
rules.notes: Evaluated worst-case: the longest timeout configured across VTY lines is used, and any 'exec-timeout 0' is treated as no timeout at all.

rules.title: Set 'enable secret' and enable 'service password-encryption'
rules.description: The privileged-exec password must be stored as a one-way hash ('enable secret'), and stored passwords elsewhere in the configuration must not be left in plaintext.
rules.rationale: 'enable password' stores the privileged password reversibly and is trivially recovered from a configuration backup. 'service password-encryption' additionally obscures line and username passwords so a copied config does not immediately yield credentials.

remediation.summary: Configure a hashed enable secret and turn on password encryption; remove the legacy enable password.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 1.4.1 Set 'password' for 'enable secret'
CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 1.4.2 Enable 'service password-encryption'
rules.notes: CIS lists these as two clauses; they are evaluated together here because either one alone still leaves privileged credentials recoverable. 'service password-encryption' uses reversible Vigenere (type 7) encoding and is a defence-in-depth measure, not a substitute for 'enable secret'.

rules.title: Unset 'private' and 'public' for 'snmp-server community'
rules.description: No SNMP community string may use a well-known default value such as 'public' or 'private'.
rules.rationale: Default community strings are the first thing an attacker tries. A readable community exposes the full device configuration and topology; a writable one permits configuration changes over UDP with no user authentication.

remediation.summary: Remove default community strings and replace them with unique, non-guessable values restricted by an ACL.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 1.5.2 Unset 'private' for 'snmp-server community'
CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 1.5.3 Unset 'public' for 'snmp-server community'
rules.notes: Comparison is case-insensitive: 'Public' is no less well-known than 'public'. Prefer SNMPv3 with authPriv over any v1/v2c community.

rules.title: Set version 2 for 'ip ssh version'
rules.description: The device must enforce SSH protocol version 2. Version 1 and the 1.99 compatibility mode are cryptographically broken.
rules.rationale: SSHv1 has structural weaknesses including a CRC-32 integrity check that permits insertion attacks. Leaving the version unset lets IOS negotiate 1.99, which allows a client to downgrade the session to v1.

remediation.summary: Generate an adequate RSA key and pin SSH to version 2.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 2.1.1.6 Set version 2 for 'ip ssh version'
rules.notes: An absent 'ip ssh version' statement is reported as NEEDS_REVIEW rather than FAIL: the effective version depends on the IOS train and on whether an RSA key exists, so it cannot be established from the configuration text alone.

rules.title: Set 'no ip http server'
rules.description: The on-box HTTP management server must be disabled.
rules.rationale: The IOS HTTP server authenticates over an unencrypted channel, exposing privileged credentials, and has a long history of remotely exploitable defects. It is rarely needed on an infrastructure device.

remediation.summary: Disable the HTTP server; use HTTPS or SSH if a management interface is genuinely required.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - section 2.1 Global Service Rules
rules.notes: Mapped at section level: this control is expressed under the benchmark's global service rules, and the exact clause number differs between IOS 15 and IOS 17 editions. Confirm the clause against your licensed copy before citing it in a formal audit.

rules.title: Configure a logging destination (syslog host or local buffer)
rules.description: Logging must be on and must have at least one destination: a remote syslog host, a sized local buffer, or both.
rules.rationale: A device that keeps no log has no incident timeline. Remote syslog additionally preserves evidence after a device is rebooted, reimaged, or compromised, which is exactly when local logs are lost.

remediation.summary: Enable logging to a sized local buffer and to a remote syslog collector.
cli: service timestamps log datetime msec show-timezone

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 2.2.2 Set 'buffer size' for 'logging buffered'
CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - 2.2.4 Set IP address for 'logging host'
rules.notes: CIS treats the buffer and the remote host as separate clauses; this rule requires at least one destination and fails the device if logging is explicitly turned off with 'no logging on'.

rules.title: Set an inbound 'access-class' on every 'line vty'
rules.description: Every VTY line must carry an inbound access-class restricting which source addresses may open a management session.
rules.rationale: Authentication is the second line of defence; reachability is the first. An unrestricted VTY line lets anyone who can route to the device attempt a login, which turns a stolen or guessable credential into a compromise and puts the management plane within reach of every host on the network.

remediation.summary: Permit only the management network, and apply the list inbound on every VTY line.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - section 1.2 Line Rules
rules.notes: Verify your own address is inside the permitted range before applying this, and keep console access available: an access-class that excludes you locks you out of the device. This control is evaluated worst-case - one VTY block without an inbound access-class fails it, because that block is the way in.

rules.title: Configure a login banner
rules.description: A banner must be displayed before or at login.
rules.rationale: The banner is what makes unauthorised access provably unauthorised. Prosecutions and disciplinary actions have failed because a device never told the intruder they were not welcome, and it costs one command.

remediation.summary: Set a login banner stating that access is restricted and activity is monitored.
cli: Authorised access only. Activity is logged and monitored.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - section 1.6 Banner Rules
rules.notes: Do not name the device, its model, its owner or its software version in the banner: that is free reconnaissance. Have the wording approved by whoever owns legal risk in your organisation.

rules.title: Set 'security passwords min-length' to 8 or more
rules.description: The device must refuse locally configured passwords shorter than eight characters.
rules.rationale: IOS enforces no minimum length at all unless told to, so nothing stops an operator setting a two-character password during a late-night change. This is the only control here that constrains what a future password may be, rather than auditing the ones already set.

remediation.summary: Enforce a minimum length for every locally configured password.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - section 1.1 Local Authentication Rules
rules.notes: This applies to passwords set after the command, not to existing ones. Re-set existing local credentials afterwards, or the control passes while short passwords remain in use.

rules.title: Configure at least one NTP server
rules.description: The device must synchronise its clock with at least one NTP time source.
rules.rationale: Every other control here produces evidence, and evidence is worth what its timestamps are worth. Without synchronised time, logs from two devices cannot be correlated, an incident timeline cannot be reconstructed, and certificate validation and time-based access rules misbehave.

remediation.summary: Point the device at two or more internal time sources.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - section 2.3 Logging Rules
rules.notes: Two sources let the device detect a lying one; a single source is a single point of failure for every timestamp it produces. Authenticate NTP (ntp authenticate / ntp trusted-key) where the time source crosses an untrusted network.

rules.title: Do not configure read-write SNMP communities
rules.description: No SNMP v1/v2c community may grant read-write access.
rules.rationale: An SNMP v1/v2c community is a password sent in cleartext, and a read-write one is a password that rewrites the configuration. Anyone who observes it once - or guesses it - can download the running-config or push a new one, without ever authenticating to the CLI.

remediation.summary: Remove every read-write community; use read-only with an ACL, or SNMPv3 for write access.

references: CIS Cisco IOS Benchmark - section 1.5 SNMP Rules
rules.notes: This is independent of the community's name: renaming a read-write community away from 'private' does not fix it. If write access is genuinely required, use SNMPv3 with authPriv rather than a v2c community.
